questions.q: What does this lesson say the honest goal should be, instead of 'zero lock-in everywhere'?
options: Refusing to use any managed service from any provider
Knowing exactly where lock-in exists, why, and whether it was a deliberate, worthwhile trade or an accident nobody evaluated
Switching cloud providers on a fixed yearly schedule regardless of cost
Building a custom abstraction layer over every single cloud service
questions.explain: The lesson reframes the goal away from eliminating lock-in entirely and toward being deliberate about where it exists and whether the trade-off was actually worth it.

questions.q: Why is favoring Kubernetes for compute described as a cheap portability bet?
options: Kubernetes is free to run on every cloud provider with no licensing cost
Kubernetes requires no infrastructure of its own to operate
Containerizing a workload is something you'd do anyway for other reasons, so the portability across AKS, EKS, and GKE comes close to a side effect rather than a separate investment
Kubernetes eliminates the need for any cloud provider entirely
questions.explain: Since containerization is good practice independent of multi-cloud, the fact that Kubernetes behaves similarly across AKS, EKS, and GKE is portability gained largely for free, not a dedicated cost center.

questions.q: What specifically transfers between clouds when a team uses Terraform, even though a module written for one provider won't run unmodified on another?
options: The exact compiled binary of the provider plugin
The declarative skill and workflow — resources, state, plan/apply, modules — which make the team productive on a new provider faster than starting from scratch
The cloud provider's billing account
The specific IP addresses assigned to virtual machines
questions.explain: Even though the HCL for one provider doesn't run against another, the declarative workflow and skill set transfer directly, which is why Terraform experience is a portability asset even across different providers.

questions.q: What does the lesson say is the main problem with building a custom internal abstraction layer over every cloud service 'just in case' a migration happens someday?
options: It has to be maintained forever by your own team, rarely covers 100% of the underlying service, and slows down every feature built on top of it, against a risk that may never materialize
It is explicitly forbidden by every major cloud provider's terms of service
It automatically triggers a provider migration every six months
It makes Kubernetes and Terraform unusable
questions.explain: Speculative abstraction layers impose permanent maintenance and slow down feature delivery, and because they rarely cover every provider feature, teams end up working around them anyway — often protecting against a migration that never happens.

questions.q: According to the lesson's working rule of thumb, when should a team build a custom abstraction layer over a cloud service?
options: Whenever a new employee joins the cloud team
As soon as any single service is adopted, regardless of plans to switch
Only on weekends, to avoid disrupting production deployments
Only when a specific, named migration is already planned — never speculatively, against an unquantified risk
questions.explain: The lesson's rule of thumb reserves custom abstraction layers for cases with an actual, named migration already planned, rather than building them speculatively against a risk nobody has evaluated.
